analysis.one_liner: Barred broadband providers from blocking, slowing, or discriminating against lawful internet content and services.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee markup or a House vote; it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written net neutrality into law. It required broadband providers to let users reach all lawful websites, apps, and services, and barred the companies that own the wires from blocking, slowing, or discriminating against unaffiliated content, or charging other companies extra to reach their customers. It also required providers to disclose speeds and limits in plain language and put enforcement in the hands of the FCC. The House committee it was sent to never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who rely on broadband from one of only two providers in most areas, would gain a legal guarantee that their provider cannot block, degrade, or favor its own services over competitors'. Small websites, startups, and e-commerce businesses would gain a level playing field: they could reach users without paying the cable or phone company for priority. Innovators and investors would gain certainty that open access would not be revoked.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Broadband users and small online businesses

how_it_helps.text: Each broadband provider would have a duty to let users access all lawful content, applications, and services, and not to block, impair, degrade, or interfere with any person's lawful use of broadband, including attaching lawful devices.

Providers could not favor their own content or services over unaffiliated ones, or impose surcharges on rival content and services, and would have to give unaffiliated providers at least equal speed and quality.
Providers would have to disclose speed, nature, and limitations of the service in plain language, so consumers could compare plans and detect problems.

The FCC would have to adopt rules letting anyone complain, with complaints deemed granted unless acted on within 90 days and cease-and-desist orders available within 48 hours of a prima facie showing — fast enforcement instead of years of litigation.

analysis.who_pays: Cable and telephone broadband companies would bear the cost: they could no longer collect fees from websites for preferential delivery, could not steer customers to their own video or voice products by degrading rivals, and would face fines or damages orders for violations. Some network-management flexibility is preserved in the exceptions.

drawbacks.text: Broadband companies and many economists argued that nondiscrimination rules could discourage investment in network capacity and slow the buildout of faster networks, since providers could not monetize premium delivery tiers.

The bill's enforcement provisions are unusually aggressive: a complaint is deemed granted if the FCC does not act within 90 days, and cease-and-desist orders must issue within 48 hours of a prima facie showing, which could produce hasty orders against providers before a full review.

Defining what counts as prohibited discrimination versus permitted reasonable network management is technically difficult, and the bill's own exceptions (security, spam, tiered speeds) leave a gray zone that the FCC rules would have had to resolve.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a legal guarantee that the two companies selling most Americans their home internet cannot pick winners and losers online — is substantial and directly protects consumers and small businesses. The costs are real but mostly hypothetical: providers keep broad network-management, security, and speed-tiering exceptions, so the main thing surrendered is the ability to charge content companies or favor their own services. The enforcement design is overly aggressive and would likely have needed tuning, but that is a drafting flaw, not a reason the whole principle fails.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its telecommunications subcommittee, which never took it up; it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the Network Neutrality Act of 2006 on May 2, 2006, joined by Reps. Eshoo, Boucher, and Inslee.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on May 2, 2006, and to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet on May 15, 2006.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearings on the bill, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote in either chamber.
Twenty-three House members cosponsored the bill, 22 Democrats and 1 Independent.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill expired without a vote.

The bill would have imposed enforceable net neutrality duties on broadband providers, including a ban on blocking, degrading, or discriminating against lawful content and on surcharges for rival services, enforced by the FCC.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable and telephone broadband providers were better off: with no law passed, they kept the freedom to manage their networks, favor their own services, and charge content companies for delivery, with no FCC net neutrality duties during that Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican House majority, which took no action.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from blocking, degrading, or discriminating against unaffiliated content and services, from favoring their own offerings, and from surcharging rival providers. The bill's own findings note that most residential consumers can choose between only two wireline providers, so these companies had little competitive pressure to stay neutral on their own.

industries.industry: Internet content, application, and e-commerce companies
industries.note: The bill's findings state the high-tech economy would be severely harmed if content providers could not reach consumers without interference from network operators. Startups and small online businesses would get guaranteed equal-quality access to users.

Users would gain enforceable rights to reach all lawful content and services, plus plain-language disclosure of speed and limits. Enforcement could order damages to complaining parties, not just regulatory fines.
